articles.title: Gloria Steinem Was the Godmother of Neoliberal Feminism
articles.author: Jenny Brown
articles.content_excerpt: Gloria Steinem, the establishment’s favorite radical feminist, died on September 2. The mainstream media has gone all out in praising her, with the Wall Street Journal and The New York Times united in their adulation. The Times called her the “personification of the women’s movement” and credited her with helping to usher in “sweeping cultural transformations across virtually every facet of American life, from the boardroom to the courtroom to the bedroom.” They approvingly quote her self-description as an “entrepreneur of social change.” For many people, she is the only radical feminist they can name, eclipsing the extraordinary women who planned and launched the successful women’s liberation movement starting in 1967. articles.title: Organizing from the Bottom: IBEW’s Fight for Sanitary Facilities
articles.author: Detroit DSA
articles.content_excerpt: Workers in high-visibility gear gather at a downtown Detroit worksite, with the city skyline visible in the background. By Kevin Szczesny To get clean Porta-johns in our workplace, construction workers at the Marriott site in downtown Detroit marched on the boss. Workers from at least seven unions of the building trades were represented, with zero union staffers or officers present. Many union halls were in support of the action, but the work and the application of leverage were entirely rank-and-file driven. As an active member of IBEW Local 58 (Electrical Workers), I often hear from sympathetic organizers who “can’t imagine how hard it must be” organizing in a largely conservative and obstinate workforce. articles.title: Ruth First’s Legacy Has Outlived the Regime That Killed Her
articles.author: Christopher J. Lee
articles.content_excerpt: In August 1982, a parcel bomb went off at the Center for African Studies at Eduardo Mondlane University in Maputo, Mozambique. Sent by the South African government’s Special Branch, its target and victim was Ruth First, a lifelong member of the South African Communist Party (SACP), who was fifty-seven years old at the time. Her assassination has since become the stuff of legend, a symbol of the violent brutality of the apartheid government toward its critics in the last decades of its existence. The murder of First was part of a broader effort by the white minority state to eliminate its opponents following the Soweto Uprising of 1976, which resulted in a revival of (and a generational shift within) the anti-apartheid struggle. articles.title: Private Equity’s Pension Heist
articles.author: Clark Randall
articles.content_excerpt: From 2024 to 2025, the two hundred largest pension funds in the United States increased their investment in private credit by 57 percent . It’s now gone up around 650 percent over the past five years. Private credit is the other side of the coin to private equity (PE) — among other things, it provides the loans for PE firms’ leveraged buyouts. The biggest PE firms have massive private credit arms that have, in recent years, overrun their private equity cores. They act as the unregulated winners of the postrecession economy, avoiding scrutiny and taking risks that commercial banks were foreclosed from under the Dodd–Frank Act. articles.title: Francis Fukuyama: The American Right Has Gone Off the Deep End
articles.author: Francis Fukuyama
articles.content_excerpt: In 1989, Francis Fukuyama wrote a sweeping philosophical polemic in which he argued that liberal democratic capitalism was the only viable economic and political system. Countries would either converge on its model or drift into dysfunction. What prevented states and individuals from accepting this fate was a fear of being the Last Man, a Nietzschean term for the individual living without ideas worth dying for. articles.title: In Serbia, Few Frankly Reckon With Ratko Mladić’s Crimes
articles.author: Lela Vujanić
articles.content_excerpt: When residents of a block in Belgrade’s city center woke up to the news last week, they were confronted with a mural celebrating a war criminal, painted overnight. Furious, they plotted a “night action” to destroy this latest tribute to Ratko Mladić with improvised defacement tactics. While the war criminal’s face is ever present across the Serbian capital, this was the first time a mural several meters long and about one meter high had appeared on the building surrounding their park. The news of Mladić’s death, while in detention at The Hague, came in the middle of a campaign for parliamentary elections that have not yet been called but according to President Aleksandar Vučić are expected any day now. articles.author: Ben Burgis
articles.content_excerpt: As summer turns into fall, the United States remains mired in a wildly unpopular war in Iran. On the home front, inflation is stubbornly persistent. articles.title: The Rise of the Billionaire Lobby
articles.author: Ben Case
articles.content_excerpt: You’ve heard of the oil lobby, the tobacco lobby, the Israel lobby, the charter school lobby. Behind all of these are billionaires who benefit from the underlying industries or sectors, and whose corporations use their resources to lobby the government for favorable policies. Now, in reaction to a California ballot initiative for the world’s first billionaire tax, we have an innovation: a lobby for billionaires themselves. Self-advocacy by wealthy people is nothing new, of course.
